Automation & Scripting for Enterprise Operations

Operational automation using Python, Shell, PowerShell, and Ansible, covering database health checks, reporting, maintenance, application monitoring, and workflow optimization.

I develop automation solutions that simplify repetitive administrative tasks, reduce manual intervention, and improve operational productivity.

My work spans database administration, application monitoring, reporting, storage management, and scheduled enterprise workflows.

Using Python, Shell, PowerShell, and Ansible, I turn recurring operational activities into repeatable processes that are easier to execute, monitor, and maintain.

Area Technologies and focus

Operational automation Ansible playbooks and reusable scripts

Measurable Workflow Improvements

Two projects delivered measurable reductions in execution time.

Workflow Before After Time saved Reduction
Control-M job 52 hours 4.5 hours 47.5 hours per execution Approximately 91%
Weekly database cloning Approximately 11 hours Approximately 6.5 hours Approximately 4.5 hours per week Approximately 41%

These figures describe the specific workflows measured, not a platform-wide performance improvement or a separately measured reduction in administrator effort.

Control-M Job Optimization

I optimized a long-running Control-M job, reducing execution time from 52 hours to 4.5 hours.

This substantially shortened the job’s processing window and improved its operational turnaround.

My broader performance work also includes optimizing long-running Hive, Spark, and HBase workloads and associated Control-M jobs to improve execution efficiency and operational reliability.

Weekly Database Cloning Automation

I developed a menu-driven workflow for weekly Oracle Database cloning.

The framework brought related operations into a centralized process, reducing repeated manual intervention and opportunities for execution errors.

Weekly execution time decreased from approximately 11 hours to 6.5 hours, saving approximately 4.5 hours each week.

Daily Health Checks and Reporting

I automated daily health checks and reporting using Python scripts and Ansible playbooks.

The objective was to consolidate recurring checks into a consistent operational view rather than requiring administrators to collect the same information manually each day.

The generated reports support routine review, exception identification, and investigation of issues requiring attention.

Completed Operational Automations

The following nine automations have been completed and are running successfully.

Their successful operation refers to the automation workflows themselves. Monitoring reports may still identify failed backups, unavailable applications, or other conditions requiring investigation.

1. Database Daily Health Report

Automated the collection and presentation of key database, application, and server-health information.

The reporting scope includes:

  • Instance status and database information.
  • Database size and space utilization.
  • ASM disk-group utilization.
  • Tablespace capacity and low-free-space checks, including checks for less than 5% available space.
  • Archive log statistics.
  • Daily RMAN backup status.
  • Top SQL queries by resource consumption.
  • Sessions with high physical I/O activity.
  • EBS Concurrent Manager status.
  • Database export-backup verification.
  • Disk-space details for database and application servers.

This provides a consolidated starting point for daily operational review and helps identify storage constraints, backup issues, and resource-intensive activity.

The reporting approach is modular, allowing additional checks, databases, and servers to be incorporated as requirements evolve.

2. Daily Auditing Reports

Automated daily auditing reports to improve visibility and traceability of database activities.

The reports support audit review and compliance-related activities without requiring the same information to be gathered manually.

The approach accommodates different database audit configurations and user-activity reporting requirements.

3. Automated Database Table Statistics Gathering

Automated statistics gathering for selected database tables to keep optimizer statistics current.

This standardizes a recurring maintenance activity and supports consistent query-optimization inputs.

Additional tables can be included as application and maintenance requirements change.

4. Daily Alert Log Monitoring

Automated database alert-log review to surface errors and warnings requiring attention.

The workflow produces log outputs that support investigation without requiring administrators to manually inspect every full alert log.

The monitoring approach can accommodate different log locations, formats, and alert levels across environments.

5. Application Availability Reporting

Automated application endpoint checks and generated reports showing availability status and response information.

The reporting includes:

  • A consolidated application-health view.
  • Working, warning, and failed status categories.
  • Response information for individual checks.
  • A separate exception report highlighting failed or warning entries.

This helps direct operational attention to services requiring investigation.

Availability results reflect the checks performed at the reporting time; they are not a guarantee of continuous application availability.

The configuration-based approach allows additional application endpoints and environments to be included.

6. Daily Table Growth Tracking

Automated daily table-growth tracking to improve visibility into changing storage consumption.

The reports support:

  • Reviewing growth trends.
  • Identifying unusual increases.
  • Planning future capacity.
  • Prioritizing storage investigations.

The approach can be reused across databases, environments, and projects.

7. Tableau Log Management

Automated Tableau log housekeeping on Windows servers to reclaim space and support reliable platform operations.

This reduces recurring manual cleanup and helps prevent unnecessary log accumulation from consuming available disk capacity.

The housekeeping approach can be adapted to other tools with similar log-management requirements.

8. Table and Tablespace Space Management

Automated space-management activities to support table growth and reduce dependence on repeated manual intervention.

The objective is to address capacity constraints before they interrupt database operations.

This complements growth tracking and low-space reporting by bringing recurring space-management work into an automated workflow.

9. Database Alert Log Management

Automated scheduled database alert-log housekeeping, including monthly purging and backup for future reference.

This is separate from daily alert-log monitoring:

  • Monitoring identifies errors and warnings.
  • Housekeeping manages accumulated log files and retained copies.

The approach can be applied across multiple database environments.

Operational Reporting in Practice

The reporting solutions bring database and application information into readable HTML outputs.

Database Reports

Database reports consolidate information such as instance state, database size, tablespace utilization, archive activity, RMAN backup status, SQL activity, physical I/O, and server storage.

Where applicable, they also include ASM information and EBS Concurrent Manager status.

Application Reports

Application reports present endpoint status and response information in a consolidated view.

A separate exception-focused report helps operators concentrate on entries requiring attention rather than reviewing every successful check individually.

Exception Visibility

The purpose of monitoring automation is not to make every report appear healthy. It is to make operational conditions visible.

A successfully generated report that identifies a failed backup or an unavailable application is performing its monitoring role.

Reusability and Extensibility

I focus on automation that can evolve with operational requirements.

Across these solutions, extension points include:

  • Adding databases and application servers.
  • Introducing new health checks.
  • Updating monitored application endpoints.
  • Expanding table lists and reporting scope.
  • Adapting log paths and housekeeping requirements.
  • Reusing scripts across environments.

This makes the work more useful than a collection of isolated, one-time scripts.
